client: I've been really struggling lately because I got assigned this major group project at university, and just thinking about it makes my chest tight and my mind start racing. The worst part is that I know it's going to involve presenting in front of the class, and public speaking is something I genuinely dread — like, it's not just nerves, it feels almost paralyzing. I'm not even sure talking about it here is going to change anything, but I figured I'd at least try.
therapist: It sounds like this project is stirring up a lot of fear and dread, and I really appreciate you showing up and giving this a try even when part of you doubts it will help — that takes courage. The physical sensations you're describing, like the tight chest and racing mind, are your body's way of signaling that something feels genuinely threatening, and those feelings make a lot of sense given how paralyzing public speaking can feel for you. I'm curious — when you imagine that presentation, what's the specific fear that tends to hit hardest: is it more about what others will think of you, losing control in the moment, or something else entirely?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, I think the biggest fear is what others will think of me — like, I have this vivid image of my mind just going completely blank mid-sentence, and everyone staring at me, and my group members looking embarrassed that they're stuck with me. It's almost like I'm already convinced it's going to go badly before it even happens. And then on top of that, I feel guilty about dreading it so much, because I know my group is counting on me and I don't want to let them down.
therapist: What you're describing — already picturing the worst outcome as if it's a certainty — is something we call a cognitive distortion, where your mind is essentially time-traveling into a future it's written as a disaster before a single word has been spoken. It's also really telling that you're carrying guilt on top of the fear, like you're not allowed to struggle without it meaning you're failing your group. I'd gently ask: if a close friend told you they were terrified of presenting, would you see them as a burden to their team, or would you see someone doing their best under real pressure?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: I know logically I'd never think of a friend that way — I'd probably want to reassure them and tell them they're going to be fine. But when it comes to myself, it just feels different, like the same rules don't apply to me for some reason. I hear what you're saying about the cognitive distortion thing, but I'm not sure just knowing it has a name actually makes the fear feel any less real in my body.
therapist: You're absolutely right that naming something doesn't dissolve the feeling — understanding that a fear is irrational and actually feeling safe are two very different things, and CBT works best when we address both the thoughts *and* the body's response together. What's really striking is that you so clearly have compassion and wisdom available for others, but there's something that blocks that same kindness from reaching you — and that double standard is often one of the most important things to gently challenge. I'm wondering, when did you first start feeling like the rules were different for you — like you somehow deserved less grace than the people you care about?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That's a hard question to sit with, honestly. I think it goes back pretty far — like, growing up I always felt like I had to earn my place in a room, whether that was at home or at school, and making mistakes felt like proof that I didn't belong there. I'm not sure how much digging into that is going to help me get through this presentation in a few weeks though — it feels kind of distant from the actual problem right now.
therapist: What you just shared is actually really significant — that feeling of having to *earn* your place, and mistakes meaning you don't belong, sounds like it might be the very root of why a blank moment on stage feels so catastrophic rather than just awkward. And your concern about staying practical is completely valid; we don't need to unpack your whole history to get you through this presentation. What if we worked on both — building some concrete tools for the next few weeks, while also noticing how that old belief might be quietly running the show when the fear spikes?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess that makes sense, and I'm willing to try, but I'm a little skeptical about the "noticing the old belief" part — like, in the moment when my heart is pounding and I've forgotten what I was going to say, I really doubt I'm going to have the headspace to reflect on childhood patterns. What kind of concrete tools are you actually talking about, because that part sounds more useful to me right now?
therapist: Your skepticism is completely fair, and honestly, the last thing you need in a high-panic moment is to be coaching yourself through a philosophy seminar — so let's get practical. Two tools that work really well together are controlled breathing (specifically a slow exhale that's longer than your inhale, which directly signals your nervous system to calm down) and a short "grounding phrase" you prepare in advance, something simple like "I know this material" that you can reach for when your mind goes blank. I'm also noticing there's a lot of energy in how you're engaging with this right now — which makes me curious, underneath the skepticism, is there a part of you that actually really wants this to go well and is maybe more invested than you're letting on?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, okay, you caught me — I do want it to go well, probably more than I've been admitting. I think part of the reason the fear is so intense is because I actually care about doing a good job, not just for my group but for myself too. The breathing thing sounds manageable, but I'm worried that in the actual moment I'll forget to do it, or it'll feel weird and obvious to everyone watching me just standing there taking deep breaths.
therapist: That moment of honesty — admitting you actually care deeply about this — is really important, because it reframes the fear as evidence of investment rather than weakness. The good news is that the breathing technique doesn't have to look like anything from the outside; a single slow, quiet exhale before you start speaking is invisible to your audience but powerful for your nervous system. And since you know you care about doing well, we can actually use that — would it help to practice the breathing *now*, in low-stakes moments, so that by the time the presentation comes it's already a familiar habit your body knows how to reach for?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Practicing it in low-stakes moments sounds doable in theory, but I'm not sure I'll actually remember to do it — like, I have good intentions about these kinds of things and then life gets busy and I just don't follow through. I guess I'm also wondering if one breathing technique is really enough to get me through something that feels this overwhelming, because the presentation is more than just the physical panic, it's the whole thing of people judging me and my mind going blank. Can we talk a bit more about what to actually do if the blank moment happens, because that's the scenario I keep replaying in my head?
therapist: The "blank moment" fear is so common and so vivid for people with presentation anxiety, and having a concrete plan for it actually tends to reduce the fear of it happening in the first place — so let's tackle it directly. If your mind goes blank, the most effective thing you can do is pause, take that quiet exhale, and say something like "let me gather my thoughts for a second" — because what feels like an eternity to you is usually just a few seconds to an audience, and most people read a brief pause as confidence rather than failure. On the follow-through concern, rather than relying on memory, what if we made the practice ridiculously small and specific — like one intentional exhale every time you sit down to work on the presentation itself, so it's already tied to something you're already doing?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: The idea of saying "let me gather my thoughts for a second" actually makes me feel a tiny bit better, because it gives me something to do instead of just freezing and panicking — like a lifeline I can grab onto. I'm still not fully convinced the audience would read it as confidence rather than failure, because in my head they're all just waiting for me to mess up. But tying the breathing to sitting down to work on the presentation is the first suggestion that's felt genuinely manageable, so I'm willing to try that one.
therapist: It's really good to hear that the "lifeline" phrase landed well, and that one suggestion finally feels genuinely within reach — that matters. I do notice though that even as you're describing feeling a little better, there's something in how you're speaking that sounds more activated than your words alone might suggest, like there's still a lot of energy or tension running underneath this. I'm wondering — is there something about today's conversation, or the presentation itself, that's stirring up more than you're quite ready to put into words yet?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very loud, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, yeah, there is something else sitting underneath all of this that I haven't said out loud yet. Part of what makes this presentation feel so unbearable is that I barely know the people in my group — I feel like an outsider already, and the thought of messing up in front of strangers who are also somehow depending on me is almost worse than messing up in front of people who know me. It's like the loneliness and the anxiety are tangled up together in a way I didn't really realize until just now.
therapist: What you just named — that the loneliness and anxiety are wrapped around each other — sounds like a really significant realization, and it took courage to say it out loud. Being evaluated by strangers carries a particular kind of vulnerability, because there's no existing relationship to cushion a mistake, no sense that they already know you're more than one stumble. I'm curious, as you sit with that realization now, does it shift anything about how you understand what this presentation has actually been representing for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think the presentation has been representing more than just public speaking — it's like a test of whether these strangers will accept me or confirm that I don't really belong there, which is a lot of pressure to put on a fifteen-minute presentation. Saying that out loud makes me feel kind of exposed, honestly, and also a little silly, because when I hear it that way it sounds like I'm making it bigger than it is. But I also can't just talk myself out of it feeling that way, so I'm not sure what to do with this realization practically.
therapist: Please don't dismiss what you just uncovered as "silly" — you've actually just identified the core belief that's been driving so much of this fear, which is that belonging has to be earned and one mistake could cost you your place, and that's a profound thing to recognize, not an overreaction. The fact that you can hear how much weight you've placed on this presentation and feel exposed saying it out loud tells me this realization is landing somewhere real and important for you. What would it mean for how you approach the presentation — and maybe even the group — if belonging wasn't actually on trial, but was something you were allowed to simply claim for yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
